vignette: Jamal, a 48-year-old fashion designer of Middle Eastern descent, had always found solace in the colorful world of fabrics and patterns. Yet, ever since the day of the factory explosion that claimed several lives, that world felt tainted, overshadowed by fear and anxiety. The disaster had been a man-made calamity, a fire ignited by negligence in a facility he once proudly collaborated with. Now, memories of that day invaded his thoughts at the most unexpected moments, dragging him back to the chaos - the acrid smoke, the screams, and the heat that seemed to engulf him. The memories were jagged and disjointed, pieces of a horrifying puzzle that refused to fit together. Each recollection felt alarmingly real, as if he were re-experiencing the event in the present rather than recalling it from the past. These intrusive memories often triggered a wave of nausea, a physical manifestation of his emotional turmoil. It was as if his body was reminding him of the terror he had endured, forcing him to confront sensations he desperately wished to avoid. Jamal would sometimes touch surfaces, feeling the temperature of objects around him, only to be transported back to the day of the explosion - the scalding heat of the flames and the icy grip of fear. In those moments, he would find himself planning escape routes, instinctively scanning his surroundings for potential dangers. Jamal had learned that when the memories returned, staying busy was the only way to keep the panic at bay. Whenever he felt the urge to escape, he threw himself into work, believing that distraction would shield him from the emotional turmoil that threatened to engulf him. He could never relax fully; he always needed to know the exits, an unshakeable habit that strained his relationships and left him feeling isolated in social settings. In a bid to cope with the overwhelming feelings that surged whenever the memories returned, Jamal resorted to maladaptive strategies. He kept himself constantly busy, burying his emotions beneath layers of design sketches and fabric swatches, believing that if he worked hard enough, he could outrun the shadows of his past. Yet, despite his frenetic activity, the memories remained alive, surfacing unexpectedly and throwing him into a spiral of despair. He would often hurt himself physically, believing that inflicting pain could provide a release from the emotional agony that threatened to consume him. Each act of self-harm was a desperate attempt to regain control over the chaos within, but it only deepened his suffering, leading him to feel even more fragmented and disconnected from himself. Jamal's life became increasingly characterized by an undercurrent of threat. He felt as though danger lurked around every corner, a constant companion that heightened his anxiety. This sense of threat exacerbated his concentration difficulties. "Each time the memories returned, even the slightest reminder would lead him to scan his environment for threats, as if those past horrors could manifest again at any moment." This sense of persistent danger pushed Jamal to adopt coping strategies like checking the locks at home multiple times, as he felt that ensuring everything was secure was the only way to manage the chaos in his mind. At work, he would find himself unable to focus on his designs as his mind raced with intrusive thoughts and images of the explosion. "These memories of the explosion not only clouded his concentration but heightened his sense of threat, making him feel a constant tension that something terrible could happen again." The fabric he once loved to manipulate now felt heavy in his hands, weighed down by his memories of that horrific day. "The unrelenting sense of threat that accompanied his memories had driven him to this moment, as he realized that he could no longer navigate his life under the weight of fear and avoidance." Whenever he tried to concentrate, the taste of smoke would return to him with vivid clarity, a reminder of the fear and panic that had engulfed him. "To cope with the overwhelming surge of emotions that followed these memories, Jamal found himself working late into the night, believing that if he kept himself busy enough, he could stave off the painful thoughts that threatened to consume him." Even the simple act of stepping outside his home became fraught with anxiety. "When the threat felt so pervasive, he resorted to checking his workspace multiple times, believing that if he ensured everything was in order, he could create a sense of control over the chaos that loomed in his mind." Each time he left, he would check locks and doors repeatedly, a compulsive behavior that stemmed from an overwhelming need to feel secure. "However, the more he engaged in these strategies, such as overworking himself or isolating from friends, the more his sense of danger intensified, as if his actions were confirming that there was indeed a threat he needed to be wary of." However, this only served to reinforce his sense of danger and the memories that plagued him. Each time he chose to avoid social situations or stayed late at work, he confirmed to himself that the threat was real and ongoing, leaving him caught in a cycle that only heightened his anxiety. "The more intense his sense of threat became, the more he felt he had to engage in these compulsive behaviors, as if each lock he checked could stave off the potential chaos looming just beyond his control." The more he succumbed to these maladaptive strategies, the more trapped he felt in his own mind, with memories that chained him to his trauma and a constant vigilance that kept him on edge. "When the memories surged forth, Jamal felt a pressing need to keep himself busy with his designs, believing that if he worked hard enough, he could stave off the anxiety that threatened to overwhelm him." Now, sitting in the therapist's office, Jamal found himself at a crossroads. "When the threat felt so pervasive, he found that his compulsive behaviors, like checking the locks multiple times, provided a temporary sense of relief, but ultimately failed to alleviate the underlying anxiety." He had come to recognize that the cycle of avoidance and self-harm was unsustainable. "His constant avoidance behaviors seemed to reinforce the feeling that danger was ever-present, making it impossible for him to trust his surroundings and feel safe." "This cycle of avoidance kept him in a heightened state of alertness, as if his actions validated the very threat he was trying to escape." "Jamal realized that by avoiding situations that reminded him of the explosion, he never allowed himself the opportunity to confront and dismantle the anxiety, which kept the fear alive and unchallenged." He feared that his life would continue to deteriorate if he didn't seek help. "This avoidance only intensified his memories of the explosion, as he found that suppressing his emotions did not lessen their vividness but instead made them more intrusive and painful." What frightened him most was the thought of being forever imprisoned by his memories, unable to reclaim the vibrant life he once led. "Yet, the more he engaged in these strategies, the more he felt ensnared by his memories, as if each avoidance only reinforced the terror that lingered just beneath the surface." As he shared his story, Jamal hoped for a path forward - a way to understand and integrate his experiences without being overwhelmed by them. The desire to regain control and find peace within himself was now an ember of hope amidst the chaos. "Whenever intrusive memories from the explosion surfaced, he found himself drowning in anxiety, which drove him to keep himself busy with work, believing that distraction would shield him from the emotional pain." "The nausea would swell within him, creating a palpable sense of danger that made him feel as though he were still trapped in that burning factory, unable to escape." In his attempt to manage this overwhelming fear, he often found himself working late into the night, thinking that if he kept himself occupied enough, he could avoid the feelings of vulnerability that came with stillness. "When the memories surged forth, Jamal found himself compelled to immerse in work, believing that staying busy was the only way to escape the suffocating anxiety that followed." "When every reminder of the explosion heightened his anxiety, he found himself slipping into workaholic tendencies, convinced that the only way to regain a semblance of normalcy was to keep his mind occupied at all costs." "To avoid the emotional pain these memories stirred within him, he began working late into the night, convincing himself that exhaustion would be the only way to escape the suffocating anxiety."

  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."

  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."

  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: There is no established link between threat and maladaptive strategies, thus missing how the sense of danger might drive Jamal to engage in avoidance behaviors.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not connect the sense of threat to memory, leaving the relationship between perceived danger and the recollection of the traumatic event unaddressed.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: There is no causal relationship shown between maladaptive strategies and memory, missing how avoidance behaviors affect the recall of traumatic experiences.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette fails to connect maladaptive strategies to threat, leaving out how coping mechanisms might reinforce feelings of danger.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Jamal, a 48-year-old fashion designer of Middle Eastern descent, had always found solace in the colorful world of fabrics and patterns. Yet, ever since the day of the factory explosion that claimed several lives, that world felt tainted, overshadowed by fear and anxiety. The disaster had been a man-made calamity, a fire ignited by negligence in a facility he once proudly collaborated with. Now, memories of that day invaded his thoughts at the most unexpected moments, dragging him back to the chaos — the acrid smoke, the screams, and the heat that seemed to engulf him. The memories were jagged and disjointed, pieces of a horrifying puzzle that refused to fit together. Each recollection felt alarmingly real, as if he were re-experiencing the event in the present rather than recalling it from the past. These intrusive memories often triggered a wave of nausea, a physical manifestation of his emotional turmoil. It was as if his body was reminding him of the terror he had endured, forcing him to confront sensations he desperately wished to avoid. Jamal would sometimes touch surfaces, feeling the temperature of objects around him, only to be transported back to the day of the explosion — the scalding heat of the flames and the icy grip of fear. In those moments, he would find himself planning escape routes, instinctively scanning his surroundings for potential dangers. Jamal had learned that when the memories returned, staying busy was the only way to keep the panic at bay. Whenever he felt the urge to escape, he threw himself into work, believing that distraction would shield him from the emotional turmoil that threatened to engulf him. He could never relax fully; he always needed to know the exits, an unshakeable habit that strained his relationships and left him feeling isolated in social settings. In a bid to cope with the overwhelming feelings that surged whenever the memories returned, Jamal resorted to maladaptive strategies. He kept himself constantly busy, burying his emotions beneath layers of design sketches and fabric swatches, believing that if he worked hard enough, he could outrun the shadows of his past. Yet, despite his frenetic activity, the memories remained alive, surfacing unexpectedly and throwing him into a spiral of despair. He would often hurt himself physically, believing that inflicting pain could provide a release from the emotional agony that threatened to consume him. Each act of self-harm was a desperate attempt to regain control over the chaos within, but it only deepened his suffering, leading him to feel even more fragmented and disconnected from himself. Jamal's life became increasingly characterized by an undercurrent of threat. He felt as though danger lurked around every corner, a constant companion that heightened his anxiety. This sense of threat exacerbated his concentration difficulties. "Each time the memories returned, even the slightest reminder would lead him to scan his environment for threats, as if those past horrors could manifest again at any moment." This sense of persistent danger pushed Jamal to adopt coping strategies like checking the locks at home multiple times, as he felt that ensuring everything was secure was the only way to manage the chaos in his mind. At work, he would find himself unable to focus on his designs as his mind raced with intrusive thoughts and images of the explosion. "These memories of the explosion not only clouded his concentration but heightened his sense of threat, making him feel a constant tension that something terrible could happen again." The fabric he once loved to manipulate now felt heavy in his hands, weighed down by his memories of that horrific day. "The unrelenting sense of threat that accompanied his memories had driven him to this moment, as he realized that he could no longer navigate his life under the weight of fear and avoidance." Whenever he tried to concentrate, the taste of smoke would return to him with vivid clarity, a reminder of the fear and panic that had engulfed him. "To cope with the overwhelming surge of emotions that followed these memories, Jamal found himself working late into the night, believing that if he kept himself busy enough, he could stave off the painful thoughts that threatened to consume him." Even the simple act of stepping outside his home became fraught with anxiety. "When the threat felt so pervasive, he resorted to checking his workspace multiple times, believing that if he ensured everything was in order, he could create a sense of control over the chaos that loomed in his mind." Each time he left, he would check locks and doors repeatedly, a compulsive behavior that stemmed from an overwhelming need to feel secure. "However, the more he engaged in these strategies, such as overworking himself or isolating from friends, the more his sense of danger intensified, as if his actions were confirming that there was indeed a threat he needed to be wary of." However, this only served to reinforce his sense of danger and the memories that plagued him. Each time he chose to avoid social situations or stayed late at work, he confirmed to himself that the threat was real and ongoing, leaving him caught in a cycle that only heightened his anxiety. The more he succumbed to these maladaptive strategies, the more trapped he felt in his own mind, with memories that chained him to his trauma and a constant vigilance that kept him on edge. Now, sitting in the therapist's office, Jamal found himself at a crossroads. He had come to recognize that the cycle of avoidance and self-harm was unsustainable. "His constant avoidance behaviors seemed to reinforce the feeling that danger was ever-present, making it impossible for him to trust his surroundings and feel safe." "Jamal realized that by avoiding situations that reminded him of the explosion, he never allowed himself the opportunity to confront and dismantle the anxiety, which kept the fear alive and unchallenged." He feared that his life would continue to deteriorate if he didn't seek help. "This avoidance only intensified his memories of the explosion, as he found that suppressing his emotions did not lessen their vividness but instead made them more intrusive and painful." What frightened him most was the thought of being forever imprisoned by his memories, unable to reclaim the vibrant life he once led. As he shared his story, Jamal hoped for a path forward — a way to understand and integrate his experiences without being overwhelmed by them. The desire to regain control and find peace within himself was now an ember of hope amidst the chaos. "Whenever intrusive memories from the explosion surfaced, he found himself drowning in anxiety, which drove him to keep himself busy with work, believing that distraction would shield him from the emotional pain." "The nausea would swell within him, creating a palpable sense of danger that made him feel as though he were still trapped in that burning factory, unable to escape." In his attempt to manage this overwhelming fear, he often found himself working late into the night, thinking that if he kept himself occupied enough, he could avoid the feelings of vulnerability that came with stillness.
